facts.claim: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite
facts.context: Sputnik 1 went up on 4 October 1957 and circled the Earth every 96 minutes.
facts.goDeeper: It was a polished metal ball about the size of a beach ball, and its radio beeps could be picked up on amateur sets in American back gardens.

facts.claim: Yuri Gagarin became the first human being to fly in space
facts.context: Gagarin made a single orbit aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961, and was back on the ground 108 minutes later.
facts.goDeeper: He did not land inside his spacecraft. He ejected at about 23,000 feet and came down by parachute, which the Soviets kept quiet for years because the record rules required a pilot to land with his craft.

facts.claim: John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth
facts.context: Glenn flew three orbits aboard Friendship 7 on 20 February 1962.
facts.goDeeper: He went back to space in 1998 aboard the shuttle Discovery, aged 77.

facts.claim: Alexei Leonov left his capsule for the first spacewalk
facts.context: Leonov spent about twelve minutes outside Voskhod 2 on 18 March 1965, on a tether.
facts.goDeeper: His suit ballooned in the vacuum until he could not bend it, and he had to bleed air out of it to get back through the airlock.

facts.claim: The Apollo 1 crew was lost in a fire during a launch-pad test
facts.context: Fire swept the sealed capsule during a rehearsal on 27 January 1967, and the three men aboard did not survive.
facts.goDeeper: The hatch opened inward and could not be shifted in time. Every Apollo hatch built afterwards swung outward and could be opened in seconds.

facts.claim: Apollo 8 carried the first people to leave Earth orbit and circle the Moon
facts.context: Borman, Lovell and Anders orbited the Moon ten times over Christmas 1968 and came home without landing.
facts.goDeeper: Anders' photograph of the Earth rising over the lunar horizon is often credited with helping start the modern environmental movement.

facts.claim: Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon
facts.context: Armstrong stepped off the ladder late on 20 July 1969, with Buzz Aldrin following about twenty minutes later.
facts.goDeeper: The lander touched down with roughly 25 seconds of fuel to spare, because Armstrong had flown on past a boulder field looking for smooth ground.

facts.claim: An oxygen tank burst on Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon
facts.context: The tank ruptured two days out, on 13 April 1970. The landing was abandoned and the crew got home four days later.
facts.goDeeper: They shut the command module down and used the lunar lander as a lifeboat: a craft built to keep two men alive for two days kept three alive for four.

facts.claim: Apollo 17 made the last crewed landing on the Moon
facts.context: Cernan and Schmitt spent three days on the surface in December 1972 and lifted off on the 14th.
facts.goDeeper: Schmitt was a geologist, the only working scientist ever to reach the Moon, and nobody has been back since.

facts.claim: American and Soviet spacecraft docked with each other in orbit for the first time
facts.context: An Apollo and a Soyuz joined up on 17 July 1975 and the two commanders shook hands through the hatch.
facts.goDeeper: The crews swapped meals and gifts and stayed docked for nearly two days. The mission is usually taken as the point where the race stopped being a race.

facts.claim: People who have walked on the Moon
facts.context: Twelve men walked on the Moon, two at a time, across six landings between 1969 and 1972.
facts.goDeeper: All twelve were American, all were military or civilian test pilots bar one geologist, and the last of them left in December 1972.

source.title: List of people who have walked on the Moon

facts.claim: Astronauts who flew the Apollo 11 mission
facts.context: Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins launched together on 16 July 1969. Two landed; one stayed in orbit.
facts.goDeeper: Michael Collins was on the far side of the Moon, out of radio contact with anyone alive, at the moment the other two touched down.

facts.claim: Days the Apollo 11 mission lasted, launch to splashdown
facts.context: Eight days and three hours, from the launch on 16 July 1969 to the splashdown in the Pacific on 24 July.
facts.goDeeper: Almost all of it was travel. The two men were on the surface for less than a day, and outside the lander for about two and a half hours.

facts.claim: Height of the Saturn V rocket that launched the Moon missions
facts.context: The Saturn V stood 363 feet tall on the pad, fully stacked.
facts.goDeeper: That is taller than the Statue of Liberty on her pedestal, and the first stage burned through roughly 13 tons of fuel every second.

facts.claim: Laika, the first dog to orbit the Earth, came home safely
facts.context: Laika flew on Sputnik 2 in November 1957 in a capsule with no way of coming back down.
facts.goDeeper: The Soviet Union said for decades that she had lived several days. In 2002 a scientist on the programme revealed she had died of overheating within hours.

facts.claim: The Great Wall of China is the only human-made structure visible from the Moon
facts.context: It is not visible from the Moon, and astronauts say it is hard to pick out even from low orbit.
facts.goDeeper: From the Moon the Earth is a bright marble a couple of inches across at arm's length. No human-made thing shows up at all.

facts.claim: NASA spent millions developing a pen that would write in zero gravity
facts.context: Paul Fisher developed the space pen privately, at his own expense, and NASA then bought them for a few dollars each.
facts.goDeeper: The punchline of the story is wrong too. The Soviets bought the same pens, and both sides had used pencils before that.

facts.claim: Armstrong meant to say 'one small step for a man', and the 'a' is not there in the recording
facts.context: Armstrong always said he intended the article, which is what makes the line mean anything; it cannot be heard on the transmission.
facts.goDeeper: He said he hoped history would grant him the missing letter. NASA's own transcript prints it in brackets.

facts.claim: The Soviet Union put the first woman in space
facts.context: Valentina Tereshkova flew alone aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963, and spent nearly three days in orbit.
facts.goDeeper: She had been recruited as a parachutist rather than a pilot, and twenty years passed before an American woman, Sally Ride, flew in 1983.

facts.claim: The Apollo 11 crew was put in quarantine after getting back to Earth
facts.context: Nobody knew whether anything harmful had come back with them, so the three were sealed away for about three weeks and released on 10 August 1969.
facts.goDeeper: They spent the first stretch in a converted airstream trailer, and the President welcomed them home by talking to them through its window.
